c.tagline: Persia's pulse beneath the snow-capped Alborz Mountains.

taxi.fareNote: Agency/telephone taxis are metered; street and shared 'khatti' taxis run fixed per-route fares - agree on price before boarding.

emergency.note: Fire: 125. English-speaking operators are not guaranteed; hotel staff can assist.

avoid.reason: Skip the Harandi/Darvazeh Ghar area south of the Grand Bazaar (drug activity), and never linger near or photograph government, military, or nuclear-linked sites.
Beware fake plainclothes 'police' demanding passports or cash, and watch for pickpockets in the Grand Bazaar and on crowded metro lines.

hood_desc: Historic core around the Grand Bazaar and Ferdowsi/Imam Khomeini squares - budget-friendly, packed with museums, banks and traditional teahouses; best for first-timers wanting to walk to sights.
Central business and shopping spine along Vali Asr/Vanak - modern towers, malls and restaurants with easy Metro access; suits business travelers and those wanting a central, convenient base.
Trendy Africa (Jordan) Street area with boutiques, cafes and galleries popular with young Tehranis and expats; suits travelers who want a hip, walkable, foreigner-friendly scene.
Traditional bazaar town at the foot of the Alborz Mountains, gateway to Darband's hiking trails and mountainside restaurants; suits travelers seeking cooler air, nature access and local atmosphere.

water.note: Technically treated and meets standards, but aging pipes and mineral content commonly cause stomach upset in visitors; bottled water advised.

transit.pay: Fares are paid with a rechargeable smart card (Tehran Metro/Bus Card) tapped at turnstiles or bus card readers; single-journey paper tickets are sold at metro stations. Cash is not accepted on board buses or at metro gates.
transit.hours: Metro runs roughly 05:30-23:00 Saturday-Wednesday, with reduced hours Thursday/Friday; no overnight service, so late-night travelers rely on taxis or ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Traffic congestion is severe at rush hour; the Metro is usually the fastest way to cross the city, and women-only carriages are available on every train.

train: Tehran Railway Station (Rah Ahan) - domestic services to Mashhad, Isfahan, Tabriz, Yazd and international connections toward Turkey

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to Azadi/Mehrabad terminal (60-75 min)
Shared/agency taxi to city center (45-60 min)

tip.r: Rounding up is appreciated in taxis and restaurants; upscale hotels/restaurants may add a service charge. Not deeply ingrained but increasingly common in tourist-facing venues.

food.name: Chelo kabab
food.desc: Iran's national plate: buttered saffron rice with a grilled fillet kabab barg or minced koobideh, a charred tomato, sumac and raw onion.

places.name: Nayeb
places.note: Part of Tehran's oldest chelo kababi line, founded in 1875 and still a benchmark.

places.name: Shamshiri
places.note: Famous for kabab barg and joojeh; arrive before 1pm to beat the queue.

places.name: Moslem Restaurant
places.note: Landmark bazaar kitchen known for enormous portions; expect to wait.

food.name: Ghormeh sabzi
food.desc: The most loved Persian stew: slow-cooked herbs blackened with fenugreek, kidney beans, lamb and whole dried limes, served over rice.

places.name: Khesht-e Behesht
places.note: Traditional house with a courtyard pool, coloured glass and curtained alcoves.

places.name: Daf Traditional Restaurant
places.note: Full stew list - ghormeh sabzi and gheymeh - alongside the kababs.

places.name: Laleh Mansion
places.note: Restored mansion serving the classic stew repertoire.

food.name: Dizi (abgoosht)
food.desc: Lamb, chickpeas and potato cooked in a stone crock; you drink the broth first, then mash the solids into a paste and eat it with flatbread.

places.name: Azari Traditional Teahouse
places.note: Grand old teahouse near the railway station with live music and a famous dizi.

places.name: Khesht-e Behesht
places.note: Serves dizi with the mashing tools and full ritual explained.

places.name: Sofrekhaneh Sonnati Sangalaj
places.note: Traditional dining hall in the old city, reliable for the lunchtime dizi.

food.name: Ash-e reshteh
food.desc: Thick green soup of herbs, beans and noodles, finished with fried mint, crisp onion and kashk whey. Sold from vats on the street in winter.

places.name: Tajrish Bazaar
places.note: Ash vats bubbling at the market entrances; served in the shadow of the shrine.

places.name: Grand Bazaar food lanes
places.note: Ash and haleem stalls tucked into the covered corridors.

places.name: Darband trail stalls
places.note: Mountain-path cafes serving ash to hikers; best in cold weather.

food.name: Tahchin and zereshk polo
food.desc: Saffron rice baked with yoghurt and egg into a crisp golden cake, or piled with tart barberries and chicken. Tehran's celebration rice dishes.

places.name: Moslem Restaurant
places.note: Its tahchin is the dish people queue on the stairs for.

places.name: Nayeb
places.note: Zereshk polo ba morgh alongside the full kabab menu.

places.name: Laleh Mansion
places.note: Traditional rice dishes in a restored courtyard setting.

food.name: Bastani sonnati and faloodeh
food.desc: Saffron and rosewater ice cream studded with frozen cream and pistachio, often served scooped over faloodeh - icy rice noodles with lime.

places.name: Akbar Mashti
places.note: The Tehran name for traditional saffron ice cream, going since the 1950s.

places.name: Tajrish Bazaar sweet shops
places.note: Several bastani counters inside and around the market.

places.name: Grand Bazaar ice cream stalls
places.note: Old-style counters serving bastani sandwiched between wafers.

food.name: Doogh
food.desc: Salted yoghurt thinned with water and scented with dried mint, sometimes lightly carbonated. The standard partner to kabab and dizi.

places.name: Azari Traditional Teahouse
places.note: House-made doogh in clay jugs to go with the dizi.

places.name: Nayeb
places.note: Poured cold with every chelo kabab order.

places.name: Tajrish Bazaar
places.note: Dairy stalls selling fresh and fizzy doogh by the bottle.

food.name: Chai and saffron sharbat
food.desc: Black tea drunk through a lump of rock candy, plus cordials of saffron, rosewater, sekanjabin or sour cherry poured over ice. All alcohol-free.

places.name: Azari Traditional Teahouse
places.note: Samovar tea, nabat sugar and live traditional music in a tiled hall.

places.name: Cafe Naderi
places.note: Tehran's literary cafe since the 1920s, still pouring tea and coffee.

places.name: Darband sharbat stalls
places.note: Mountain-path sellers with jars of sekanjabin, sour cherry and saffron cordial.

landmarks: Azadi Tower
Tehran's monumental white marble gateway landmark, blending Achaemenid and Islamic architecture, and an unmistakable symbol of the city.
Milad Tower
One of the world's tallest telecommunication towers, offering a revolving restaurant and sweeping 360-degree views over the entire city.
Golestan Palace
A UNESCO World Heritage Qajar-era palace complex dazzling with mirrored halls, tiled facades, and opulent royal gardens.
Tehran Grand Bazaar
A sprawling historic labyrinth of covered lanes selling carpets, spices, and jewelry, the vibrant commercial soul of old Tehran.
Sa'dabad Complex
A vast leafy royal estate of over a dozen palaces built by the Qajar and Pahlavi dynasties, now open as museums amid mountain scenery.
Niavaran Palace Complex
The last royal residence of the Pahlavi dynasty, an elegant palace and gardens offering a glimpse into pre-revolution Iran.
Tabiat Bridge
An award-winning, sinuous pedestrian bridge connecting two parks, celebrated as a modern architectural icon of contemporary Tehran.
National Museum of Iran (Iran Bastan Museum)
Iran's premier archaeological museum, housing treasures spanning millennia from Persepolis reliefs to ancient Persian artifacts.
Tochal
A dramatic Alborz mountain peak reached by a scenic telecabin, offering ski slopes, hiking, and stunning views above the smog line.
Darband
A picturesque mountainside village at the foot of the Alborz range, beloved for its cafes, streams, and hiking trails with skyline views.

intl.to: Van (Turkey), with onward Lake Van ferry + TCDD connection toward Tatvan/Ankara
intl.op: Raja / Islamic Republic of Iran Railways (RAI)

train.note: The Tehran–Van sleeper (departs Tehran roughly twice weekly) resumed in 2025 after a multi-year halt; it is a genuine overnight service and includes a ferry across Lake Van before the Turkish leg. Booking on raja.ir often needs an Iran-based connection/VPN and can be easier via the station or an agent.

intl.op: Iranian coach companies from Terminal-e Gharb — tickets at the terminal, no English booking site
Iranian coach companies from Terminal-e Gharb — tickets at the terminal

bus.note: International coaches leave from Tehran's western terminals (Terminal-e Gharb) for Istanbul (Turkey) and, for pilgrims, toward Najaf/Karbala (Iraq), but there is no single official English booking site — tickets are bought through Iranian bus companies/agents at the terminal. Check current border and travel conditions before relying on these.

ferry.note: Tehran is far inland with no ferries. Iran's international Persian Gulf ferries (e.g. to Sharjah/Dubai, UAE) run from Bandar Abbas via Valfajr Shipping, roughly 1,300 km south.

half.name: Mount Damavand
half.blurb: Iran's highest peak, a snow-capped volcano drawing climbers, hikers and thermal-spring seekers.

half.name: Qom
half.blurb: Major pilgrimage city centered on a magnificent golden-domed shrine and religious schools.

half.name: Qazvin
half.blurb: Former Safavid capital with historic mosques, mansions and gateway to Alamut valley.

full.name: Kashan
full.blurb: Desert-edge city known for grand historic houses, bazaars and a serene garden.
